NONPROFIT PUBLIC BENEFIT CORPORATION ARTICLES OF INCORPORATION
Prepared for Acme Community Fund

NONPROFIT PUBLIC BENEFIT CORPORATION PURPOSE DECLARATION
The name of the corporation is Acme Community Fund. Acme Community Fund is a nonprofit public benefit corporation and is not organized for the private gain of any person. It is organized under the Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law for the following purposes: providing after-school educational programs to underserved youth. The initial street address of Acme Community Fund is 500 Market St, San Francisco, CA 94105.

REQUIRED CONTENT OF NONPROFIT PUBLIC BENEFIT CORPORATION ARTICLES
California's Nonprofit Corporation Law contains its own, separate required-content statute for a nonprofit public benefit corporation's articles of incorporation, distinct from the required-content statute that governs an ordinary for-profit corporation. The nonprofit statute requires the filed articles to state: the corporation's name; a specific statutorily prescribed statement that the corporation "is a nonprofit public benefit corporation and is not organized for the private gain of any person" and is organized under the Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law for "public" or "charitable" purposes (or both) — with a further description of the corporation's purposes mandatory if "public" purposes are elected and optional in all other cases (a narrow exception substitutes a different, Government Code-prescribed purpose statement for a corporation that is itself a public bank); the name and California street address of the corporation's initial agent for service of process; the corporation's initial street address; and its initial mailing address, if that differs from the street address. Unlike the required content for an ordinary for-profit corporation's articles, nothing in this list calls for a statement of authorized shares — a nonprofit public benefit corporation has no shareholders and issues no stock.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "The articles of incorporation of a corporation formed under this part shall set forth: (a) The name of the corporation. (b) (1) Except as provided in paragraph (2), the following statement: “This corporation is a nonprofit public benefit corporation and is not organized for the private gain of any person. It is organized under the Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law for (public or charitable [insert one or both]) purposes.” [If the purposes include “public” purposes, the articles shall, and in all other cases the articles may, include a further description of the corporation’s purposes.]"
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 5130(a)-(b)(1), California Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law, the required name and statutory purpose statement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=5130.)
  "(c) The name and street address in this state of the corporation’s initial agent for service of process in accordance with subdivision (b) of Section 6210. (d) The initial street address of the corporation. (e) The initial mailing address of the corporation, if different from the initial street address."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 5130(c)-(e), California Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law, agent for service of process and required addresses (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=5130.)

The two citations below are subsections of the same statutory section, Cal. Corp. Code § 5130, so they are treated as one source, not two independent ones.

STATE PURPOSE STATEMENT VS. THE FEDERAL 501(C)(3) ORGANIZATIONAL TEST
California's required purpose statement for a nonprofit public benefit corporation's articles and the Internal Revenue Code's tax-exemption purpose language are two different legal requirements from two different governments, layered on top of each other rather than one flowing from the other. The state formation statute requires only the fixed statutory sentence that the corporation "is a nonprofit public benefit corporation... organized under the Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law for (public or charitable) purposes" — it does not use the word "exclusively," and it does not itself require the specific language the IRS looks for. That more specific language comes from federal law: 26 U.S.C. § 501(c)(3) grants tax-exempt status only to corporations "organized and operated exclusively for religious, charitable, scientific, testing for public safety, literary, or educational purposes" (among a few other listed purposes), and a federal Treasury regulation implementing that statute — the "organizational test" — requires an organization's articles to limit its purposes to one or more of those exempt purposes and not expressly empower it to engage, beyond an insubstantial part of its activities, in activities that are not in furtherance of an exempt purpose. A California nonprofit public benefit corporation's articles can fully satisfy the state's own formation statute while still needing additional, more specific purpose language to satisfy this separate federal test — the state statute does not require that federal-test language, and satisfying the state statute is not the same as satisfying the federal one.

  "“This corporation is a nonprofit public benefit corporation and is not organized for the private gain of any person. It is organized under the Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law for (public or charitable [insert one or both]) purposes.”"
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 5130(b)(1), California Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law, the state's own purpose-statement requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=5130.)
  "Corporations, and any community chest, fund, or foundation, organized and operated exclusively for religious, charitable, scientific, testing for public safety, literary, or educational purposes, or to foster national or international amateur sports competition... or for the prevention of cruelty to children or animals, no part of the net earnings of which inures to the benefit of any private shareholder or individual..."
  — 26 U.S.C. § 501(c)(3), Internal Revenue Code, the federal tax-exemption purpose requirement (https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title26-section501&num=0&edition=prelim)

(a) Limit the purposes of such organization to one or more exempt purposes; and (b) Do not expressly empower the organization to engage, otherwise than as an insubstantial part of its activities, in activities which in themselves are not in furtherance of one or more exempt purposes."
  — Treas. Reg. § 1.501(c)(3)-1(b)(1)(i), Federal tax regulation, the organizational test articles-of-organization requirement (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-26/chapter-I/subchapter-A/part-1/subject-group-ECFR062882ac6495890/section-1.501(c)(3)-1)

Corp. Code § 5130.

THE DISSOLUTION-OF-ASSETS CLAUSE: NOT A CALIFORNIA FILING REQUIREMENT
The specific, dedicated-assets dissolution clause that commonly appears in nonprofit articles of incorporation — stating that upon dissolution the corporation's remaining assets will be distributed to another nonprofit organization, or to a federal, state, or local government, for a public purpose — is not one of the items California's own nonprofit-articles content statute (Cal. Corp. Code § 5130, covered above) requires. That statute's required-content list runs to five items — name, purpose statement, agent, street address, mailing address — and a dissolution or asset-distribution clause is not among them. A dissolution-related provision does appear in California's Nonprofit Corporation Law, but only as an optional clause available in one narrow situation: for a subordinate corporation created under a head organization's authority, the articles may (not must) provide that the corporation dissolves when the head organization revokes its charter, and that upon such a dissolution its assets will be distributed to that head organization. Separately, when a nonprofit public benefit corporation actually dissolves for any reason, a different statute governs how its assets are in fact disposed of: in conformity with the corporation's own articles or bylaws, subject to the terms of any trust under which the assets are held, and ordinarily only by a superior court decree issued in a proceeding to which the California Attorney General is a party (or, alternatively, upon the Attorney General's written waiver of objection). The specific "distribute to another exempt organization or government entity, never to members" language is instead a federal tax-law requirement: a Treasury regulation implementing 26 U.S.C. § 501(c)(3) treats an organization's assets as properly "dedicated to an exempt purpose" — a condition of the same organizational test discussed above — only if, on dissolution, they would go by the articles or by operation of law to another exempt purpose, to a government for a public purpose, or to a court-selected organization; that same regulation states the test fails outright if the articles or state law would let dissolution assets go to the organization's own members or shareholders.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "That in the event of its dissolution pursuant to an article provision allowed by subparagraph (A) or in the event of its dissolution for any reason, any assets of the corporation after compliance with the applicable provisions of Chapters 15 (commencing with Section 6510), 16 (commencing with Section 6610) and 17 (commencing with Section 6710) shall be distributed to the head organization."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 5132(a)(2)(B), California Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law, the narrow optional dissolution provision for subordinate corporations (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=5132.)
  "(a) Except as provided in Section 6715, all of a corporation’s assets shall be disposed of on dissolution in conformity with its articles or bylaws subject to complying with the provisions of any trust under which such assets are held. (b) Except as provided in subdivision (c), the disposition required in subdivision (a) shall be made by decree of the superior court of the proper county in proceedings to which the Attorney General is a party."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 6716(a)-(b), California Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law, how assets are actually disposed of upon dissolution (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=6716.)
  "An organization is not organized exclusively for one or more exempt purposes unless its assets are dedicated to an exempt purpose... However, an organization does not meet the organizational test if its articles or the law of the State in which it was created provide that its assets would, upon dissolution, be distributed to its members or shareholders."
  — Treas. Reg. § 1.501(c)(3)-1(b)(4), Federal tax regulation, the organizational test's dissolution-of-assets requirement (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-26/chapter-I/subchapter-A/part-1/subject-group-ECFR062882ac6495890/section-1.501(c)(3)-1)

STATUTORY PROHIBITION ON DISTRIBUTIONS
California's Nonprofit Corporation Law contains a distinct, freestanding statutory prohibition that has no counterpart in the state's general for-profit corporation statute: "No corporation shall make any distribution," subject only to a narrow carve-out for the purchase of a membership in a limited-equity housing cooperative organized as a public benefit corporation. This sits in its own chapter of the Nonprofit Corporation Law titled "Distributions," under an article titled "Limitations." A separate section of the same law gives specific people standing to go to court over a violation of a nonprofit's charitable character: the corporation itself (or a member suing in the corporation's name), an officer, a director, a person with a reversionary, contractual, or property interest in trust-held assets, or the California Attorney General, may bring an action to enjoin, correct, obtain damages for, or otherwise remedy a breach of a charitable trust, and the Attorney General must be given notice of any such action brought by the other listed parties and may intervene in it.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "No corporation shall make any distribution. This section shall not apply to the purchase of a membership in a limited-equity housing cooperative, as defined in Section 33007.5 of the Health and Safety Code, which is organized as a public benefit corporation."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 5410, California Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law, the prohibition on distributions (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=5410.)
  "Notwithstanding Section 5141, any of the following may bring an action to enjoin, correct, obtain damages for or to otherwise remedy a breach of a charitable trust: (1) The corporation, or a member in the name of the corporation pursuant to Section 5710. (2) An officer of the corporation. (3) A director of the corporation. (4) A person with a reversionary, contractual, or property interest in the assets subject to such charitable trust. (5) The Attorney General, or any person granted relator status by the Attorney General. The Attorney General shall be given notice of any action brought by the persons specified in paragraphs (1) through (4), and may intervene."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 5142(a), California Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law, who may sue to enforce a charitable trust (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=5142.)

Code § 5142, and are treated as two independent sources, not subsections of one section.

NONPROFIT CORPORATION NAMING RULES MIRROR THE GENERAL CORPORATION LAW
California's Nonprofit Corporation Law has its own naming statute for a nonprofit public benefit corporation, separate from the naming statute that governs an ordinary for-profit corporation — but on the actual statutory text, the two impose essentially the same restrictions rather than materially different ones. The nonprofit statute provides that the Secretary of State will not file articles setting forth a name containing "bank," "trust," "trustee," or related words unless a certificate of approval from the Commissioner of Financial Protection and Innovation is attached, and that a nonprofit corporation's name cannot be one the Secretary of State determines is likely to mislead the public, and must be distinguishable in the Secretary of State's records from the names of other corporations, qualified foreign corporations, and reserved or registered names. Those are the same two substantive restrictions — the financial-institution-word restriction and the misleading/distinguishability restriction — that apply to an ordinary for-profit corporation's name. The one naming feature that does not carry over is not, on inspection, a nonprofit-specific difference either: the for-profit statute's requirement that a name include "corporation," "incorporated," or "limited" (or an abbreviation) applies only to a for-profit corporation that elects close-corporation status under a share-structure-based statute that has no nonprofit counterpart — a nonprofit public benefit corporation, having no shares and no close-corporation election available to it, was never within reach of that requirement in the first place.

citations.quote: The Secretary of State shall not file articles setting forth a name in which “bank,” “trust,” “trustee,” or related words appear, unless the certificate of approval of the Commissioner of Financial Protection and Innovation is attached thereto.

citations.cite: California Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law, the misleading-name and distinguishability requirement
citations.quote: The name of a corporation shall not be a name that the Secretary of State determines is likely to mislead the public and shall be distinguishable in the records of the Secretary of State from all of the following: (1) The name of any corporation. (2) The name of any foreign corporation authorized to transact intrastate business in this state.

expectedJSON.gap: This is one state's naming statute, not a claim about naming rules in any other state — restricted words, and whether any designator word must be included in a nonprofit corporation's name at all, vary by state. This clause is also a direct correction of an assumption worth stating plainly: on the statutory text actually found, California's nonprofit naming rules do not differ in substance from the state's general for-profit corporation naming rules — both restrict the same categories of names for the same reasons, and the one difference initially expected (a designator-word requirement) turns out never to have applied to nonprofit corporations under either statute. The two citations below are subsections of the same statutory section, Cal. Corp. Code § 5122, and are treated as one source, not two independent ones.
